analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and public display of Social Security numbers to fight identity theft.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the bill without a single dissenting vote in July 2004, but three other committees kept extending their review of it until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005, and the House never voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for governments and companies to sell, buy, or publicly display a living person's Social Security number, with exceptions for law enforcement, national security, taxes, and a few other uses. It would have stopped printing Social Security numbers on government checks, driver's licenses, and employee ID cards; stopped credit bureaus from selling people's numbers through "credit header" data; and made it an unfair trade practice for a business to refuse service to someone who won't hand over their number. It also tightened how Social Security cards are issued, capping replacement cards and requiring independent verification of birth records, and created new criminal penalties for SSN misuse. The House Ways and Means Committee approved it 33-0, but the bill never reached the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, whose Social Security numbers would no longer be for sale, printed on public documents, or resold by credit bureaus — cutting off the raw material identity thieves use to open accounts in someone else's name. Businesses that do not trade in personal data would also gain, since they could no longer be forced to choose between a customer's SSN and the sale.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday consumers and identity theft victims

how_it_helps.text: Bars federal, state, and local governments and bankruptcy trustees from selling or publicly displaying anyone's Social Security number — closing the channel by which numbers collected for public programs end up on the open market.
Prohibits printing SSNs on government checks, driver's licenses, and motor vehicle registrations, and on employee ID cards — practices that expose the number to anyone who sees the document.

Makes it a felony, punishable by up to five years in prison, to sell, buy, or publicly display a living person's SSN, or to use it to track down someone to physically harm them or steal their identity.

Blocks credit bureaus from selling a person's SSN through 'credit header information' except inside a full credit report issued under the Fair Credit Reporting Act — a key source of numbers for identity thieves.
Makes it an unfair trade practice for a business to refuse service to a customer who will not hand over their SSN, unless federal law specifically requires it.

Tightens the front door of the system: states would have to independently verify birth records used to get an SSN, and replacement cards would be capped at three per year and ten for life, with stiffer criminal penalties for SSA employees who fraudulently issue cards.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and information resellers, whose business selling SSNs and credit header data would have been outlawed, along with credit bureaus; also governments and employers, which would bear the cost of changing how they issue checks, licenses, and ID cards and of securing the numbers they hold.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on businesses and governments: employers, banks, credit bureaus, and every level of government would have had to change how they store, display, and share SSNs, and the bill requires the Attorney General to weigh that cost against the benefit when writing regulations.

The Attorney General's broad authority to create additional exceptions by regulation meant the effectiveness of the ban depended heavily on how one administration chose to write the rules — the same discretion that preserved legitimate uses could also open loopholes.

Restricting credit header data and SSN sales would have limited some lawful and socially accepted uses, such as genealogy research, historical records access, and locating people for legal proceedings like child support enforcement — though the bill carved out exceptions for law enforcement and public-health research.
Key provisions took effect only a year after final Attorney General regulations were issued, so even if enacted, the protections would have been delayed while the rulemaking ran its course.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were real and large for anyone whose number gets exposed — identity theft victims spend years untangling fraudulent debts, and this bill attacked the two main channels of leakage: public records sold openly and credit headers resold separately from full reports. The carve-outs for law enforcement, insurers, and tax purposes were reasonably careful, though the Attorney General's discretion to add new exceptions and the one-year delay until final regulations were genuine weak points. The main cost was compliance — companies and governments changing systems, records, and documents — and some lawful uses (genealogy, historical research, journalism involving SSN records) would have been restricted. On balance the bill would have shifted real, recurring harm away from ordinary people and onto businesses that profit from reselling personal identifiers. Its failure meant none of those protections happened; Congress instead passed a weaker, narrower provision in 2004's intelligence law, and the SSN remained an open key to Americans' finances.

outcome.mechanism: The Ways and Means Committee passed it unanimously, but three other House committees kept getting extensions to review their portions of the bill until the two-year Congress ran out, and the House never voted on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 25, 2003 with 31 original cosponsors from both parties, led by Rep. E. Clay Shaw Jr. (R-FL), chairman of the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security.

It was sent to three committees at once; subcommittees in Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Energy and Commerce took it up in the summer of 2004, and the Ways and Means subcommittee forwarded it by voice vote.
On July 21, 2004 the full Ways and Means Committee ordered the bill reported without a single dissenting vote, 33-0, and it was reported as amended on September 14, 2004 (H. Rept. 108-685).

Because portions of the bill fell under three other committees, the House sent it sequentially to Judiciary, Financial Services, and Energy and Commerce with deadlines — and granted those committees five rounds of extensions through December 10, 2004.
No committee ever finished its review, the House never took up the bill, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, killing the bill.
Congress.gov records no further action on H.R. 2971 in any later Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and governments that sell, buy, or openly display Social Security numbers — data brokers, credit bureaus reselling credit header files, and record sellers — were better off, because the restrictions that would have ended that business died in committee without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and credit header resellers

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan: the bill had 46 cosponsors split 26 Democrats and 20 Republicans, and cleared the Ways and Means Committee 33-0 with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: Companies that buy and resell Social Security numbers — used for skip tracing, background lookups, and marketing — would lose their core product line, with felony penalties for violations. The number they sell is the master key to a person's finances, so their loss was the public's gain.

The bill amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act to stop credit bureaus from furnishing a person's SSN through standalone 'credit header' data, which could only be released inside a full credit report for permissible purposes.

The bill preserves an explicit exception letting state motor vehicle agencies sell SSNs to auto insurers for claims investigation and commercial license verification, so insurers keep access to numbers the public loses access to.

They could no longer print SSNs on employee ID badges or refuse business to customers who decline to share the number, forcing changes to records and verification practices — a real compliance cost that buys customers less exposure to theft.
